opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the main drawback is that you're leaving a lot of value on the table. A lot of these companies have spent years, sometimes decades, accumulating data that's very specific to their business: internal documents, customer interactions, code, logs, processes. That data is really their competitive advantage. When you just call a closed model through an API, you can do some prompting or retrieval on top, but you can't truly adapt the model to your domain. The model never really learns from your data in a deep way.

What we see in practice is that if you take a strong open model and fine-tune it, or even do continued pre-training on that proprietary data, you can often get a much smaller model that outperforms a much larger general-purpose model on the tasks the company actually cares about. And because it's smaller, it's cheaper and faster to serve, which matters a lot when you go to production at scale.

There's also the control aspect. With a closed model, you depend entirely on the provider. They can change the model, deprecate a version, change pricing, and your whole pipeline can shift under you. Many companies, especially in regulated industries like finance, healthcare, and defense, also aren't comfortable sending sensitive data to a third-party API. They want to deploy on their own infrastructure, on-prem or in their own cloud, and keep full ownership of both the data and the resulting model.

So the way we see it, the model should become an asset of the company, something they own and keep improving with their data over time, rather than a generic service everyone else also has access to. If everyone uses the same off-the-shelf model, it's hard to differentiate. Your data is what makes you different, and you want a model that reflects that.

r001.rationale: The response says companies leave value on the table when they use closed models, because those models cannot truly adapt to or deeply learn from the companies’ accumulated domain-specific data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main drawback is that you end up renting intelligence instead of owning it. When you call a closed API, the model you get is a generic model. It was trained on the internet, on whatever the provider decided to put in, and it knows nothing specific about your business. And the thing is, for most companies, the valuable part is not the general capability. The general capability is becoming a commodity. The valuable part is the data they have accumulated over ten, twenty years: the support tickets, the internal documents, the code, the transactions, the way their experts actually reason about problems. That data is their moat, and with a closed model they cannot really use it.

Yes, you can do some prompting, some retrieval, maybe some light fine-tuning through an API, but you are always working at the surface. You cannot change the weights in a meaningful way, you cannot do continued pre-training on your corpus, you cannot distill into a smaller model that runs cheaply on your own infrastructure. So you hit a ceiling very quickly, and that ceiling is decided by someone else.

There is also the dependency problem. The provider can change the model, deprecate it, change the pricing, change the terms. Your product is built on something you do not control and cannot even inspect. If the behavior shifts, you find out when your users complain. And for many companies, especially in Europe, in finance, in healthcare, there is the question of where the data goes. Sending your most sensitive information to a third party to get a generic answer back is not a great trade.

So what we see is that the companies that take this seriously want open weights. They want to take a strong base model, train it further on their own data, keep it on their own machines, and over time build something that is genuinely theirs and that gets better the more they use it. That compounding effect is what you give up with closed models. You pay every month and at the end you own nothing.

r001.rationale: The response says closed models are generic and that companies cannot really use their accumulated business data with them.

astra-6.text: The drawback is that you have all this domain-specific data, but the model hasn’t learned from it. You can put some of that information in the context, and that can be useful, but it’s different from being able to train the model on your data and adapt it to your particular use case. With a closed model, you’re limited to whatever customization the provider allows. So the data that could give your company an advantage may be difficult to fully exploit.

r001.rationale: The response says the model has not learned from the company’s domain-specific data and that closed-model customization limits how fully the company can exploit it.

sol-6.1.text: The main drawback is that you’re not really taking advantage of your own data. If you’re using the same model as everybody else, including your competitors, it’s difficult to build something differentiated. But you may have accumulated years of very valuable, domain-specific data. You want to be able to adapt the model to that data, to make it really good at your particular task. With a closed model, your ability to do that depends on what the provider lets you do. With an open model, you have much more control over the training and deployment, and you can turn that data into a real advantage.

r001.rationale: It says off-the-shelf closed models keep companies from taking full advantage of their accumulated domain-specific data.
